tells: Each frame is built as its own scene: an isometric traffic jam with smog, a triptych of emitters (factory, burger, battery) on three purples, an isometric map of energy tiles, a four-panel split of bird characters, a stage scene, and a car beside a UI gauge. The film is choreographed scene by scene, not one slide layout repeated.
The palette is deliberate and saturated: violet, cyan, magenta and acid yellow, with the emissions always drawn as one dark plum blob. The colour carries the story.
The bird cast is consistent and has personality (headphones, sunglasses, glasses). The character design is owned by the studio, not clip-art.
The illustration is dense, with secondary detail everywhere: trees, cables, banners, smoke puffs, rim shading and soft drop shadows. Flat vector is done at studio level.
There is very little type. The 'Goodbye CO₂!' sign is hand-placed and in character, but the type plays almost no structural role.
gaps: Find a single conceptual hook beyond 'carbon is bad, birds explain it'. Entry C ties every shot to one cosmic-eye metaphor; this one is a well-made explainer.
Give the typography a voice: titling or kinetic type woven into the isometric worlds instead of one sign card.
Move beyond the house flat-vector lighting. Add atmospheric depth, volumetric smog or one cinematic lighting shift so the climax lands emotionally.

tells: This is a vertical, social-format cut of a recognisable studio house style: a villain at a STOP console in front of a world map, a stylised topographic map of Europe, bird characters playing a memory card game, and a magenta mammoth.
The illustration is professional: tonal shading on the mammoth, layered contour map, consistent character language and a strong saturated palette.
The title 'Europe's Next Ice Age' is set in a heavy rounded sans with an outline over the map. It is legible but generic.
The burned-in captions ('completely due', 'misconception', 'ice age,') are small default subtitles that sit badly on the art. This is a repurposed short, not a designed piece.
Only 4 frames are shown, so evidence of choreography is limited. The cuts read as visual metaphors laid over narration rather than as composed motion.
gaps: Design the type for the vertical format instead of auto-captioning. Integrate the words into the frames at a real scale, as C does with its credits.
Compose for 9:16 natively. Several frames are crops of wider illustrations with dead space at the top and bottom.
Push past the house look with an unexpected device, material or lighting idea so the piece is memorable on its own.

tells: A single controlling metaphor runs through the whole film: crater to nebula, iris to seed, nautilus, accretion disc, DNA, and the eye inside the Helix Nebula. Cosmic and organic scales rhyme, and that idea belongs to this title alone.

The light and material are real: wet iris fibres, nacre and stripes on the shell resting in footprinted sand, the fibrous DNA strand, and backlit dust. Every frame has depth of field and motivated light.
Choreography between frames: circular forms (crater, pupil, shell spiral, disc, eye) carry the eye through the cuts as match-cuts in a rotational rhythm.

The typography is restrained and correct for credits: small widely tracked caps with tiny role labels, placed in the negative space of each composition. The tracked 'C O S M O S' locks around the pupil, with the 'O' becoming the eye.
The palette moves from cold slate through warm sand and bone to the nebula's ember orange. It is a controlled arc, not a single accent colour.
gaps: The credit typography is functional and could take more risk. A face with more character or a stronger scale moment before the end lock-up would lift it.
Some imagery (DNA helix, accretion disc) leans on familiar science-documentary iconography. One or two less expected metaphors would sharpen originality.
The ending eye-in-nebula lock-up is close to a known visual trope. A more surprising final transformation would make it unforgettable.

defects: Several holds where almost nothing moves: 19 of 29 seconds barely change from the second before. The 1979-vs-2012 disc comparison is identical across its 1/6 s pair, so the key reveal plays as a slide.
The 18.1 s bar-chart shot is one linear build. Bars grow left to right at a constant rate under a stepping year counter, with no change of scale, camera or emphasis to mark 2007 or 2012.

The year counter and the bars are out of step. The readout says 2024 while bars reach about 2026. In another frame the counter reads 2009 at 5.26 while the newest bar is still growing at about 2.8, so the number does not match what the chart shows.
The '2007 · 4.27' callout and leader line pop on. They appear between the paired frames with no build or ease.
The display serif sets the hyphen in 'long-term' with loose spacing, so it reads as 'long - term'.
The title card mixes alignments: the kicker and the red italic line sit flush left while the headline is centred, so the left edge is ragged.
The end card leaves most of the frame empty and puts small source text low-left. It looks like a document page, not a designed outro.
The Voronoi ice background is static, flat-shaded and vignetted. The cells do not crack, drift or thin, so they add texture without telling the story.
The 100% crop is clean: no banding or aliasing on the bar edges. But the gridlines are almost invisible and one bar's rounded top cap does not match the square caps on the others.
gaps: Choreography and pace: three long shots that each play one linear animation. Top work would use the data as camera and transition material: the disc shrinking from 1979 to 2012, bars collapsing into the trendline, ice cells breaking up as the years count down. It would also cut much faster and stress the record-low moments with timing.

Sound: the spectrogram shows a looping stack of steady synth harmonics in blocks of about 3.5 to 4 s, with gaps that line up with the cuts at 3.5 s, about 10 s and about 21 s. Apart from one noise swell near 10.5 s, there is no sound design for the bars, counter ticks or reveals, and very little dynamic arc. It reads as a generated bed, not a scored piece.

Finish and data integrity: clean, restrained editorial typography, but the counter and bars disagree, callouts pop on, and the hyphen spacing and alignment are loose. Holds have no secondary motion, such as parallax, light or subtle drift, so the piece looks like animated slides, not a film.
